Date: April 2021
Abstract.

Consider an irreducible Markov chain which satisfies a ratio limit theorem, and let ρ\rho be the spectral radius of the chain. We investigate the relation of the the ρ\rho\,-Martin boundary with the boundary induced by the ρ\rho\,-harmonic kernel which appears in the ratio limit. Special emphasis is on random walks on non-amenable groups, specifically, free groups and hyperbolic groups.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
60G50; 60J05

1. Introduction

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be the denumerable state space of a time-homogeneous Markov chain (Xn)n≥0(X_{n})_{n\geq 0} with transition matrix PP. We assume that it is irreducible and aperiodic: for any pair of points x,y∈𝒳x,y\in\mathcal{X}, there is kx,y∈ℕk_{x,y}\in\mathbb{N} such that p(n)​(x,y)>0p^{(n)}(x,y)>0 for all n≥kx,yn\geq k_{x,y}\,, where p(n)​(x,y)p^{(n)}(x,y) denotes the nn-step transition probability from xx to yy. We will often (but not always) also assume that PP has finite range, that is, for each x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, there are only finitely many yy with p⁡(x,y)>0p(x,y)>0. (This simplifies parts of the technicalities.) We choose and fix a root e∈𝒳e\in\mathcal{X}. In case of a group, this will be the identity.

In a variety of cases, part of which will be displayed below, one knows that a ratio limit theorem holds, that is, there is a function (kernel) h:𝒳2→(0,∞)h:\mathcal{X}^{2}\to(0,\infty) such that

(1.1) limn→∞p(n)​(x,y)p(n)​(e,e)=h⁡(x,y)for all ​x,y∈𝒳.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{p^{(n)}(x,y)}{p^{(n)}(e,e)}=h(x,y)\quad\text{for all }\;x,y\in\mathcal{X}\,.

Now let ρ=ρ⁡(P)=lim supp(n)​(x,y)1/n\rho=\rho(P)=\limsup p^{(n)}(x,y)^{1/n} be the so-called spectral radius of the Markov chain. It is independent of xx and yy by irreducibility. If (1.1) holds then in a large variety of cases (including finite range) one deduces that

(1.2) P​h=h​P=ρ⋅hPh=hP=\rho\cdot h

in the sense of matrix products. In particular, for any fixed yy, the function x↦h⁡(x,y)x\mapsto h(x,y) is a positive ρ\rho\,-harmonic function: more generally, for real t≥ρt\geq\rho, a function f:𝒳→ℝf:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} is tt-harmonic, if

(1.3) ∑wp⁡(x,w)​f​(w)=t​f​(x)for all ​x∈𝒳.\sum_{w}p(x,w)f(w)=t\,f(x)\quad\text{for all }\;x\in\mathcal{X}.

When t=1t=1, one just speaks of a harmonic function. Let us write ℋ+​(P,t)\mathcal{H}^{+}(P,t) for the convex cone of positive tt-harmonic functions.

For each xx, we have h⁡(x,y)≤Cx​h​(e,y)h(x,y)\leq C_{x}\,h(e,y) for all yy, where 1/Cx=ρk​p(k)​(e,x)1/C_{x}=\rho^{k}\,p^{(k)}(e,x) with the smallest kk such that this is non-zero. Therefore, we can consider the normalised ratio limit kernel

H⁡(x,y)=h⁡(x,y)/h⁡(e,y),H(x,y)=h(x,y)/h(e,y),

and the function y↦H⁡(x,y)y\mapsto H(x,y) is bounded by CxC_{x} for each yy.

(1.4) Definition.

The ratio limit compactification11 1  [11] calls this the full ratio limit compactification. 𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X}) of 𝒳\mathcal{X} is the (up to homomorphism) unique compact Hausdorff space which contains 𝒳\mathcal{X} as a discrete, dense subset and has the following properties:

  • •

    each function H⁡(x,⋅)H(x,\cdot) extends continuously to 𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X})\,, and denoting the extended kernel also by HH,

  • •

    if ξ,η∈ℛ⁡(𝒳)=𝚫ratio​(𝒳)∖𝒳\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X})=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X})\setminus\mathcal{X} are distinct, then there is x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} such that H⁡(x,ξ)≠H⁡(x,η)H(x,\xi)\neq H(x,\eta).

For the general construction of such a compactification, within the present context see e.g. [30, Thm. 7.13]. At least when PP has finite range, each function x↦H⁡(x,ξ)x\mapsto H(x,\xi), ξ∈𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\xi\in\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X})\,, is ρ\rho\,-harmonic.

In relation with his current work on Cuntz algebras related to random walks, Adam Dor-On, in an exchange that lead to the “companion” paper [11], has asked how one can describe this compactification in terms of a given structure of the underlying state space, and how it relates with the ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification. His questions were motivated by operator algebraic issues, and the answers provided here help with clarifying some of them. The Martin boundary will be recalled in the next section.

The main interest is in the case when 𝒳=Γ\mathcal{X}=\Gamma is a finitely generated, infinite group, and the Markov chain is a random walk induced by a finitely supported probability measure μ\mu on Γ\Gamma, that is,

p⁡(x,y)=μ⁡(x−1​y).p(x,y)=\mu(x^{-1}y)\,.

Irreducibility & aperiodicity then amount to the property that the support of μ\mu generates Γ\Gamma as a semi-group and that it is not contained in a coset of a proper normal subgroup of Γ\Gamma. Given the first of those two properties, the second will certainly hold if μ⁡(e)>0\mu(e)>0, where ee is the group identity. (Assuming this is not a crucial restriction.)

If in this case we have a ratio limit theorem, then clearly h⁡(g​x,g​y)=h⁡(x,y)h(gx,gy)=h(x,y) for all x,y,g∈Γx,y,g\in\Gamma, so that the function f⁡(x)=h⁡(x,e)f(x)=h(x,e) is ρ\rho\,-harmonic, and h⁡(x,y)=f⁡(y−1​x)h(x,y)=f(y^{-1}x). In that case, the ratio limit boundary is a Γ\Gamma-space, and the elements of Γ\Gamma act continuously on 𝚫ratio​(Γ)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\Gamma).

For random walks on groups, a famous ratio limit theorem is due to Avez:

(1.5) Theorem. [2]

If the group Γ\Gamma is amenable and μ\mu is symmetric, i.e., μ⁡(x−1)=μ⁡(x)\mu(x^{-1})=\mu(x), then

limn→∞p(n)​(x,y)p(n)​(e,e)=1for all ​x,y∈Γ.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{p^{(n)}(x,y)}{p^{(n)}(e,e)}=1\quad\text{for all }\;x,y\in\Gamma\,.

(Finite support is not needed here.) In this case, we see that 𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X}) is the one-point compactification. We mention here that there are symmetric random walks on amenable groups where the Martin boundary (and even the minimal one; see §2) is infinite. For example, for random walks on lamplighter groups over ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} (d≥3d\geq 3), the Poisson boundary is non-trivial, see Kaimanovich and Vershik [21], whence there are non-constant minimal harmonic functions. This is even true for certain lamplighter random walks over ℤ\mathbb{Z}, see [31].

For non-amenable groups, there is a variety of results which go beyond ratio limit theorems, namely, local limit theorems which provide an asymptotic evaluation of the nn-step transition probabilities. Typically (but not necessarily), they are of the form

(1.6) p(n)​(x,y)∼C​β​(x,y)​ρn​n−αas ​n→∞,p^{(n)}(x,y)\sim C\,\,\beta(x,y)\,\rho^{n}\,n^{-\alpha}\quad\text{as }\;n\to\infty\,,

where ∼\sim means that the quotient of the left and right hand sides tends to 11, and C,β⁡(x,y),α>0C,\beta(x,y),\alpha>0. For results up to 2000, see [29, Ch. III] and the references therein. The first of those results are due to Gerl [15] and Sawyer [27], concerning random walks on free groups, resp. regular trees. The latest results are by Gouëzel [17], [18] and Dussaule [12], for hyperbolic, resp. relatively hyperbolic groups. In between, there is a rather large body of work.

Whenever one has (1.6), this yields the ratio limit theorem with h⁡(x,y)=β⁡(x,y)/β⁡(e,e)h(x,y)=\beta(x,y)/\beta(e,e), and the kernel for the ratio limit compactification is H⁡(x,y)=β⁡(x,y)/β⁡(e,y)H(x,y)=\beta(x,y)/\beta(e,y), where ee is the group identity.

In the present paper, we exhibit classes of random walks on non-amenable groups where the ratio limit compactifictation coincides with the ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification, and one has a geometric description of the latter. Recall that ρ<1\rho<1 on those groups by Kesten [22].

After laying out some necessary preliminaries in §2, in §3 we consider free groups and regular trees, and instead of stating and proving right away the most general result for general finite range random walks, we proceed step by step. Subsequently, in §4, we consider hyperbolic groups. In §5, we discuss how the ratio limit compactification interacts with taking direct or Cartesian products. In §6, we discuss the reduced ratio limit boundary and show that in the cases of §3, there is no reduction, while for hyperbolic groups, reduction may come only from a (finite) torsion subgroup. The final §7 contains a brief discussion and an outlook on work to be done in the future.

It is on purpose that three different methods are displayed for (1) isotropic random walks on trees, (2) finite range random walks on free groups, and (3) symmetric random walks on hyperolic groups (with finite range). In spite of the fact that the most modern approach is based on the cited work of Gouëzel [17], the older methods regarding (1), going back to Sawyer [27], resp. (2), going back to Derriennic [10] plus Lalley [23], are still very valid in the author’s view. Also, for the time being, (3) does not cover (1) and (2) completely.

2. Preliminaries; the Martin compactification

A. The tt-Martin compactification
We let t≥ρt\geq\rho (focusing on the case when t=ρt=\rho). To describe the tt-Martin compactification, consider for real z>0z>0 the Green function

G⁡(x,y|z)=∑n=0∞p(n)​(x,y)​zn,x,y∈𝒳.G(x,y|z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p^{(n)}(x,y)\,z^{n}\,,\quad x,y\in\mathcal{X}\,.

The radius of convergence of this power series is r=1/ρr=1/\rho. At that value, the series may either converge or diverge for all x,yx,y. The latter is the ρ\rho\,-recurrent case, the former the ρ\rho\,-transient one. The quotient

F⁡(x,y|z)=G⁡(x,y|z)G(y,y,|z)=∑n=0∞f(n)​(x,y)​znF(x,y|z)=\frac{G(x,y|z)}{G(y,y,|z)}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f^{(n)}(x,y)\,z^{n}

is also a generating function: f(n)​(x,y)f^{(n)}(x,y) is the probability that the Markov chain starting at xx first reaches yy at time n≥0n\geq 0. It is known [30, Lemma 3.66] that F⁡(x,y|1/ρ)F(x,y|1/\rho) is always finite. In the case of a random walk on a group, it is known that one always has the ρ\rho\,-transient case, except when that group is virtually ℤ\mathbb{Z} or ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, see e.g. Woess [29, Thm. 7.8]. For real t≥ρt\geq\rho, the tt-Martin kernel is

K⁡(x,y|t)=F⁡(x,y|1/t)F⁡(e,y|1/t).K(x,y|t)=\frac{F(x,y|1/t)}{F(e,y|1/t)}.

Here we shall mainly work with t=ρt=\rho. For fixed yy, the function x↦K⁡(x,y|ρ)x\mapsto K(x,y|\rho) satisfies (1.3) at every x∈𝒳∖yx\in\mathcal{X}\setminus y. Furthermore, for fixed xx, we have K(x,⋅|t)≤CxK(x,\cdot|t)\leq C_{x} with the same bound as above. Thus, we can construct the compactification 𝚫Mart,t​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{Mart},\,t}(\mathcal{X}) of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, analogous to the one of Definition 1.4, for the tt-Martin kernel K⁡(x,y|t)K(x,y|t) in the place of H⁡(x,y)H(x,y). This is the tt-Martin compactification, and ℳt​(𝒳)=𝚫Mart,t​(𝒳)∖𝒳\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X})=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{Mart},\,t}(\mathcal{X})\setminus\mathcal{X} is the tt-Martin boundary. Each function x↦K⁡(x,ξ|t)x\mapsto K(x,\xi|t), ξ∈ℳt​(𝒳)\xi\in\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X}), is tt-harmonic. The significance of ℳt​(𝒳)\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X}) lies in the fact that every positive tt-harmonic function ff on 𝒳\mathcal{X} has an integral representation

f(x)=∫ℳt​(𝒳)K(x,⋅|t)dνf,f(x)=\int_{\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X})}K(x,\cdot|t)\,d\nu^{f}\,,

where ν\nu is a Borel measure on ℳt​(𝒳)\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X}). That measure is unique, if we require that νf​(ℳt​(𝒳)∖ℳt,min​(𝒳))=0\nu^{f}\bigl(\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X})\setminus\mathcal{M}_{t,\min}(\mathcal{X})\bigr)=0, where ℳt,min​(𝒳)\mathcal{M}_{t,\min}(\mathcal{X}) is the minimal boundary: a positive tt-harmonic function ff is called minimal, if f⁡(e)=1f(e)=1 and it cannot be written as a convex combination of two distinct positive tt-harmonic functions with value 11 at ee. The minimal boundary is {ξ∈ℳt(𝒳):K(⋅,ξ|t) is minimal}\{\xi\in\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X}):K(\cdot,\xi|t)\text{ is minimal}\,\}; it consists of all minimal tt-harmonic functions.

The finite range assumption simplifies a few things (for example, it yields that all extended Martin kernels are tt-harmonic in the first variable), but is not needed for the construction and properties. Also, aperiodicity is not needed, irreducibility is sufficient, that is, for every pair x,y∈𝒳x,y\in\mathcal{X} there is k=kx,yk=k_{x,y} such that p(k)​(x,y)>0p^{(k)}(x,y)>0. (It even suffices to have this only for ee and every yy.)

For all these facts, see e.g. [29, §24] or the references provided there. The largest part of the literature is on the ordinary 11-Martin compactification. There is a simple tool to pass from the tt-Martin compactification to the latter. Namely, take one positive tt-harmonic function ff and use the Doob transform: define new transition probabilities by

(2.1) pf​(x,y)=p⁡(x,y)​f​(y)t​f​(x)p^{f}(x,y)=\frac{p(x,y)f(y)}{t\,f(x)}

Then the tt-Martin compactification of the original Markov chain is the 11-Martin compactification of the Doob transform, and KPf(x,⋅|1)=K(x,⋅|t)/f(x)K_{P^{f}}(x,\cdot|1)=K(x,\cdot|t)/f(x).

B. Comparing compactifications
Let 𝚫⁡(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}) and 𝚫′​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\prime}(\mathcal{X}) be two compactifications of the countable set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, that is, compact Hausdorff spaces which contain 𝒳\mathcal{X} as open and dense subsets. Then we say that the former is bigger than the latter, if the identity map on 𝒳\mathcal{X} extends to a continuous surjection 𝚫​(𝒳)→𝚫′​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X})\to\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\prime}(\mathcal{X}). Clearly, if also 𝚫′​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\prime}(\mathcal{X}) is bigger than 𝚫⁡(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}) then that continuous mapping is a homeomorphism. In this case, we say that the two compactifications coincide geometrically.

In typical cases, one has a “natural” geometric compactification of 𝒳\mathcal{X} and then wants to show that it coincides geometrically with the Martin compactification, or that it is smaller than the Martin compactification.

In particular, we want to compare the ratio limit compactification with the ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification. In its geometric, resp. topological meaning, this will mean that the latter is bigger than the former, or that they coincide in the above sense.

However, this is not the full picture; it does note yet fully reflect its analytic properties. One should also ask whether in that case the homoeomorphism τ:𝚫Mart,ρ​(𝒳)→𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\tau:\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{Mart},\,\rho}(\mathcal{X})\to\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X}), in case it exists, is such that

(2.2) K⁡(x,ξ|ρ)=H⁡(x,τ⁡(ξ))for all ​x∈𝒳,ξ∈ℳρ​(𝒳).K(x,\xi|\rho)=H\bigl(x,\tau(\xi)\bigr)\quad\text{for all }\;x\in\mathcal{X},\xi\in\mathcal{M}_{\rho}(\mathcal{X})\,.

When we have two geometrically equal compactifications constructed via two different kernels, let us say that they coincide analytically, when the extended kernels coincide on the boundary. (“Coincide” is of course meant in terms of a homeomorphism as above.)

Indeed, no matter whether the ratio limit and ρ\rho\,-Martin compactifications coincide geometrically or not: whenever ν\nu is a Borel measure on the ratio limit boundary ℛ\mathcal{R}, the function

f⁡(x)=∫ℛH⁡(x,⋅)​𝑑νf(x)=\int_{\mathcal{R}}H(x,\cdot)\,d\nu

is positive ρ\rho\,-harmonic, and the above question basically amounts to asking whether every positive ρ\rho\,-harmonic function arises in this way.

In general, it is for example known that for any two finite range, irreducible random walks on a free group, the Martin compactifications coincide geometrically, but in general by no means analytically.

(2.3) Proposition.

[25, Prop. 1] Let P,QP,Q be two irreducible transition operators on 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that every positive harmonic function for PP is also harmonic for QQ. Suppose that

  • •

    the 11-Martin compactifications of PP and QQ coincide geometrically, and

  • •

    the 11-Martin boundary of PP is Dirichlet-regular, that is, every continuous function on the boundary has a continuous extension to the entire compactification which is 11-harmonic for PP on 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Then the two compactifications coincide analytically, so that the positive 11-harmonic functions for PP and QQ coincide.

We shall apply this below.

3. Trees and free groups

Let 𝕋\mathbb{T} be the regular tree where each vertex has q+1q+1 neighbours, with q≥2q\geq 2.

If there is an edge between the vertices x,y∈𝕋x,y\in\mathbb{T} then we write x∼yx\sim y. For any pair of vertices x,yx,y, there is a unique finite geodesic π⁡(x,y)=[x=x0,x1,…,xk=y]\pi(x,y)=[x=x_{0}\,,x_{1}\,,\dots,x_{k}=y] connecting the two, that is, xi−1∼xix_{i-1}\sim x_{i}, and all xix_{i} are distinct. The distance between xx and yy is then d⁡(x,y)=kd(x,y)=k. An infinite ray is a one-sided infinite geodesic path π=[x0,x1,x2,…]\pi=[x_{0}\,,x_{1}\,,x_{2}\,,\dots], that is, xk∼xk−1x_{k}\sim x_{k-1} and all xkx_{k} are distinct. Two rays π\pi and π′\pi^{\prime} are called equivalent, if they differ only by finitely many initial vertices. An end of 𝕋\mathbb{T} is an equivalence class of rays. The geometric boundary ∂𝕋\partial\mathbb{T} is the set of all ends. For any x∈𝕋x\in\mathbb{T} and ξ∈∂𝕋\xi\in\partial\mathbb{T}, there is a unique ray π⁡(x,ξ)\pi(x,\xi) starting at xx which represents ξ\xi. We set 𝚫ends​(𝕋)=𝕋∪∂𝕋\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T})=\mathbb{T}\cup\partial\mathbb{T}\,.

We choose and fix a root vertex ee. For x∈𝕋x\in\mathbb{T}, we let |x|=d⁡(e,x)|x|=d(e,x). We define the branch of 𝚫ends​(𝕋)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}) at xx as

𝚫ends​(𝕋x)={w∈𝚫ends​(𝕋):x∈π⁡(e,w)}.\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}_{x})=\{w\in\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}):x\in\pi(e,w)\}.

The topology on 𝚫ends​(𝕋)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}) is discrete on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, while a neighbourhood basis of ξ∈∂𝕋\xi\in\partial\mathbb{T} is given by the collection of all 𝚫ends​(𝕋x)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}_{x}), where x∈π⁡(e,ξ)x\in\pi(e,\xi). Each of those sets is open and compact. This turns 𝚫ends​(𝕋)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}) into a totally disconnected, compact Hausdorff space in which 𝕋\mathbb{T} is open and dense. It can be metricised as follows. For distinct v,w∈𝚫ends​(𝕋)v,w\in\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}), their confluent v∧wv\wedge w is the vertex on π⁡(e,v)∩π⁡(e,w)\pi(e,v)\cap\pi(e,w) furthest from the root ee. Then

ϑ⁡(v,w)={q−|v∧w|,if​v≠w,0,if​v=w\vartheta(v,w)=\begin{cases}q^{-|v\wedge w|}\,,&\text{if}\;v\neq w,\\ 0\,,&\text{if}\;v=w\end{cases}

is an ultrametric which induces the above topology. Below, we shall also need the Busemann function or horocycle index with respect to an end ξ∈∂𝕋\xi\in\partial\mathbb{T}. For a vertex x∈𝕋x\in\mathbb{T}, this is

𝔥⁡(x,ξ)=d⁡(x,x∧ξ)−|x∧ξ|=lim𝕋∋y→ξd⁡(x,y)−|y|.\mathfrak{h}(x,\xi)=d(x,x\wedge\xi)-|x\wedge\xi|=\lim_{\mathbb{T}\ni y\to\xi}d(x,y)-|y|.

A. Isotropic random walks on 𝕋\mathbb{T}
A Markov chain with transition matrix PP on 𝕋\mathbb{T} is called an isotropic random walk, if p⁡(x,y)p(x,y) depends only on d⁡(x,y)d(x,y). For d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, let PdP_{d} be the stochastic transition matrix with entries

pd​(x,y)={1(q+1)​qd−1,if​d​(x,y)=d,0,otherwise.p_{d}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{(q+1)q^{d-1}}\,,&\text{if}\;d(x,y)=d\,,\\[3.0pt] 0\,,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Also, we set P0=IP_{0}=I. For each dd, there is a polynomial P^d​(t)\widehat{P}_{d}(t) of degree dd such that Pd=P^d​(P1)P_{d}=\widehat{P}_{d}(P_{1}). If PP is isotropic then it can be written as a (possibly infinite) convex combination P=∑d=0∞ad​PdP=\sum_{d=0}^{\infty}a_{d}\,P_{d}\,. In order to guarantee irreducibility & aperiodicity, we assume that ad>0a_{d}>0 for some odd and some even dd. We now refer to the results explained in [29, §19.C], due to [27]. The spherical transform of PP is

P^​(t)=∑d=0∞ad​P^d​(t).\widehat{P}(t)=\sum_{d=0}^{\infty}a_{d}\,\widehat{P}_{d}(t)\,.

Thus, P=P^​(P1)P=\widehat{P}(P_{1}). It is very well known that

(3.1) ρ(P1)=2​qq+1 and ρ=ρ(P)=P^(ρ(P1)).\rho(P_{1})=\frac{2\sqrt{q}}{q+1}\and\rho=\rho(P)=\widehat{P}\bigl(\rho(P_{1})\bigl).

Let

(3.2) φ(n)=(1+q−1q+1n)q−n/2,n∈ℕ0.\varphi(n)=\Bigl(1+\frac{q-1}{q+1}n\Bigr)q^{-n/2}\,,\quad n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\,.

Set Φ⁡(x,y)=φ⁡(d⁡(x,y))\mathit{\Phi}(x,y)=\varphi\bigl(d(x,y)\bigr). Thus, Φ⁡(x)=Φ⁡(x,e)\mathit{\Phi}(x)=\mathit{\Phi}(x,e) is the spherical function which satisfies P1​Φ​(x)=ρ⁡(P1)​Φ​(x)P_{1}\mathit{\Phi}(x)=\rho(P_{1})\,\mathit{\Phi}(x). (“Spherical” means that it is an eigenfunction of P1P_{1} with value 11 at ee that depends only on |x||x|.) We see that also P​Φ​(x,y)=ρ​Φ​(x,y)P\mathit{\Phi}(x,y)=\rho\,\mathit{\Phi}(x,y). The local limit theorem of [27] says that

p(n)(x,y)∼CΦ(x,y)ρnn−3/2,as n→∞.p^{(n)}(x,y)\sim C\,\mathit{\Phi}(x,y)\,\rho^{n}\,n^{-3/2}\,,\quad\text{as }\;n\to\infty\,.

Thus, we get

H⁡(x,y)=Φ⁡(x,y)Φ⁡(e,y).H(x,y)=\frac{\mathit{\Phi}(x,y)}{\mathit{\Phi}(e,y)}.
(3.3) Theorem.

For isotropic PP as above, suppose that it has super-exponential moments: lim supd→∞ad1/d=0\limsup_{d\to\infty}a_{d}^{1/d}=0. Then the ratio limit compactification coincides with the ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification analytically. Geometrically, this is the end compactification, and for ξ∈∂𝕋\xi\in\partial\mathbb{T},

K(x,ξ|ρ)=H(x,ξ)=q−𝔥(x,ξ)/2.K(x,\xi|\rho)=H(x,\xi)=q^{-\mathfrak{h}(x,\xi)/2}.
Proof.

It is known from [18, Thm. 1.3] that under the super-exponential moment condition the ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification coincides geometrically with the end compactification.

From (3.2), we compute for any end ξ∈∂𝕋\xi\in\partial\mathbb{T}

limy→ξH(x,y)=limy→ξ1+q−1q+1​d​(x,y)1+q−1q+1​|y|q−d(x,y)/2+|y|/2=q−𝔥(x,ξ)/2.\lim_{y\to\xi}H(x,y)=\lim_{y\to\xi}\frac{1+\frac{q-1}{q+1}d(x,y)}{1+\frac{q-1}{q+1}|y|}q^{-d(x,y)/2+|y|/2}=q^{-\mathfrak{h}(x,\xi)/2}.

This shows that the ratio limit compactification coincides geometrically with the end compactification. Thus, what is left to show is that

(3.4) K(x,y|ρ)=q−𝔥(x,ξ)/2.K(x,y|\rho)=q^{-\mathfrak{h}(x,\xi)/2}.

For this purpose, we use Proposition 2.3. Since P=P^​(P1)P=\widehat{P}(P_{1}), equation 3.1 implies that ℋ+​(P1,ρ⁡(P1))⊂ℋ+​(P,ρ)\mathcal{H}^{+}\bigl(P_{1},\rho(P_{1})\bigr)\subset\mathcal{H}^{+}(P,\rho). The Green function for P1P_{1} is very well known, see e.g. [29, Lemma 1.12]. In particular,

GP1(x,y|1/ρ(P1))=2​qq−1q−d(x,y)/2,G_{P_{1}}\bigl(x,y|1/\rho(P_{1})\bigr)=\frac{2q}{q-1}q^{-d(x,y)/2},

so that (3.4) holds for P1P_{1}\,, whose Martin compactification is of course again the end compactification of 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

The spherical function Φ⁡(x)=Φ⁡(x,e)\mathit{\Phi}(x)=\mathit{\Phi}(x,e) is in ℋ+​(P1,ρ⁡(P1))\mathcal{H}^{+}\bigl(P_{1},\rho(P_{1})\bigr). We now consider the Doob transforms Q1=P1ΦQ_{1}=P_{1}^{\mathit{\Phi}} and Q=PΦQ=P^{\mathit{\Phi}}, that is, their respective matrix elements are

q1​(x,y)=p1​(x,y)​Φ​(y)ρ⁡(P1)​Φ​(x)​ and ​q​(x,y)=p⁡(x,y)​Φ​(y)ρ​Φ​(x)q_{1}(x,y)=\frac{p_{1}(x,y)\mathit{\Phi}(y)}{\rho(P_{1})\,\mathit{\Phi}(x)}\and q(x,y)=\frac{p(x,y)\mathit{\Phi}(y)}{\rho\,\mathit{\Phi}(x)}

Then f∈ℋ⁡(P,ρ)f\in\mathcal{H}(P,\rho) if and only if f/Φ∈ℋ⁡(Q,1)f/\mathit{\Phi}\in\mathcal{H}(Q,1), and analogously for P1P_{1} and Q1Q_{1}. This implies that ℋ⁡(Q1,1)⊂ℋ⁡(Q,1)\mathcal{H}\bigl(Q_{1},1\bigr)\subset\mathcal{H}(Q,1). In view of Proposition 2.3, we need to verify that the 1-Martin boundary ∂𝕋\partial\mathbb{T} is Dirichlet regular for Q1Q_{1}. By Cartwright et al. [8], for this it is necessary and sufficient that the Green kernel of Q1Q_{1} vanishes at infinity, that is,

lim|x|→∞GQ1​(x,e|1)=0.\lim_{|x|\to\infty}G_{Q_{1}}(x,e|1)=0.

Now, GQ1​(x,y|1)=GP1​(x,y|1/ρ⁡(P1))​Φ​(y)/Φ⁡(x)G_{Q_{1}}(x,y|1)=G_{P_{1}}\bigl(x,y|1/\rho(P_{1})\bigr)\mathit{\Phi}(y)/\mathit{\Phi}(x). Thus,

GQ1​(x,e|1)=2​qq−1/(1+q−1q+1​|x|)→0,as ​|x|→∞.G_{Q_{1}}(x,e|1)=\frac{2q}{q-1}\bigg/\Bigl(1+\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|\Bigr)\to 0\,,\quad\text{as }\;|x|\to\infty\,.

This concludes the proof. ∎

(3.5) Remark.

It seems likely that the super-exponential moment condition may be relaxed here. Cartwright and Sawyer [6] have shown that ℋ+​(P,1)=ℋ+​(P1,1)\mathcal{H}^{+}(P,1)=\mathcal{H}^{+}(P_{1}\,,1) for arbitrary isotropic PP, as long as it is irreducible. However, the 11-Martin compactification is the end compactification (and thus coincides analytically with the one of P1P_{1}) only under additional hypotheses, such as first moment, i.e., ∑dd​ad<∞\sum_{d}d\,a_{d}<\infty\,. Otherwise, the 11-Martin boundary can contain further, non-minimal elements. [6] contains no analogous result at the critical value ρ\rho, where also the Martin boundary might behave more “critically”. On the other hand, isotropic random walks on 𝕋\mathbb{T} are a rather special case, where more general results may hold.

B. Nearest neighbour random walk on free groups
Let 𝔽=𝔽s\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{s} be the free group on ss free generators a1,…,asa_{1}\,,\dots,a_{s}, and write a−i=ai−1a_{-i}=a_{i}^{-1}. Let I={±1,…,±s}I=\{\pm 1,\dots,\pm s\} and S={ai:i∈I}S=\{a_{i}:i\in I\}. Recall that every element xx of 𝔽\mathbb{F} can be written as a reduced word over SS,

(3.6) x=ai1ai2⋯aik,il∈I,il≠−il−1.x=a_{i_{1}}a_{i_{2}}\cdots a_{i_{k}}\,,\quad i_{l}\in I\,,\;i_{l}\neq-i_{l-1}\,.

The length |x||x| of xx is kk, and when k=0k=0, this is the empty word ee, which is the group identity. The Cayley graph of 𝔽\mathbb{F} with respect to SS is the tree 𝕋=𝕋2​s−1\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{T}_{2s-1}\,: its vertex set is 𝔽\mathbb{F}, and x,y∈𝔽x,y\in\mathbb{F} are connected by an edge whenever x−1​y∈Sx^{-1}y\in S. Thus, the natural geometric compactification F^\widehat{F} of 𝔽\mathbb{F} is the end compactification of 𝕋\mathbb{T}, with boundary ∂𝔽=∂𝕋\partial\mathbb{F}=\partial\mathbb{T}.

We now let μ\mu be a probability measure on 𝔽\mathbb{F} whose support is 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)={e}∪S\operatorname{\sf supp}(\mu)=\{e\}\cup S. This nearest neighbour case serves as a warm-up for the next sub-section; it might be omitted but may be instructive. The local limit theorem and the involved ρ\rho\,-harmonic function have been studied in detail by Gerl and Woess [16]. One has (1.6) with α=3/2\alpha=3/2, and ρ<1\rho<1 by non-amenability of 𝔽\mathbb{F}. We subsume those facts which are needed here. (The notation is slightly modified.) By group invariance, G⁡(x,y|z)=G⁡(e,x−1​y|z)G(x,y|z)=G(e,x^{-1}y|z). The function G⁡(z)=G⁡(x,x|z)G(z)=G(x,x|z) is solution of an implicit equation, which leads to a formula for ρ\rho. Set Fi​(z)=F⁡(e,ai|z)F_{i}(z)=F(e,a_{i}|z) for i∈Ii\in I. If x∈𝔽x\in\mathbb{F} has the reduced representation (3.6) then

F(e,x|z)=Fi1(z)⋯Fik(z).F(e,x|z)=F_{i_{1}}(z)\cdots F_{i_{k}}(z).

The ends of the tree 𝕋\mathbb{T} which is the Cayley graph of 𝔽\mathbb{F} can be written as infinite words

(3.7) ξ=aj1aj2aj3⋯,jl∈I,jl≠−jl−1,\xi=a_{j_{1}}a_{j_{2}}a_{j_{3}}\cdots\,,\quad j_{l}\in I\,,\;j_{l}\neq-j_{l-1}\,,

and the nthn^{\textrm{th}} vertex on the geodesic π⁡(e,ξ)\pi(e,\xi) is xn=aj1aj2⋯ajnx_{n}=a_{j_{1}}a_{j_{2}}\cdots a_{j_{n}}\,. For any t≥ρt\geq\rho, the tt-Martin compactification is ∂𝕋\partial\mathbb{T}. This goes back to Dynkin and Malyutov [13] and Cartier [4].

With ξ\xi as above, if x∈𝔽x\in\mathbb{F} has reduced representation (3.6), then there is a maximal index m=m⁡(x,ξ)≤km=m(x,\xi)\leq k such that j1=i1,…,jm=imj_{1}=i_{1}\,,\dots,j_{m}=i_{m}. Then xm=x∧ξx_{m}=x\wedge\xi in the above description of confluents in the geometry of the tree. Then the Martin kernel at ξ\xi is

K⁡(x,ξ|t)=F−ik(1/t)F−ik−1(1/t)⋯F−im+1(1/t)Fi1(1/t)Fi2(1/t)⋯Fim(1/t)K(x,\xi|t)=\frac{F_{-i_{k}}(1/t)F_{-i_{k-1}}(1/t)\cdots F_{-i_{m+1}}(1/t)}{F_{i_{1}}(1/t)F_{i_{2}}(1/t)\cdots F_{i_{m}}(1/t)}

It is always minimal. The analysis of [16] yields that in a neighbourhood of the principal singularity r=1/ρr=1/\rho, for z∈ℂ∖[r,∞)z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus[r\,,\,\infty), one has Puiseux series expansions of the form

(3.8) G⁡(z)=α0−β0​r−z+h.o.t.​ and ​Fi​(z)=αi−βi​r−z+h.o.t.,G(z)=\alpha_{0}-\beta_{0}\sqrt{r-z}+\textit{h.o.t.}\and F_{i}(z)=\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i}\sqrt{r-z}+\textit{h.o.t.}\,,

(3.11) Corollary.

For an aperiodic nearest neighbour random walk on the free group 𝔽\mathbb{F}, the ratio limit kernel is H⁡(x,y)=β⁡(x−1​y)/β⁡(y)H(x,y)=\beta(x^{-1}y)/\beta(y). The ratio limit compactification coincides analytically with the ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification, which geometrically is the end compactification 𝔽^=𝚫ends​(𝕋)\widehat{\mathbb{F}}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T})\,.

Proof.

The expansion (3.10) yields the following local limit theorem, see [16, Thm. 2]:

p(n)(e,x)∼12​ρ​πβ(x)ρnn−3/2.p^{(n)}(e,x)\sim\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\rho\,\pi}}\,\beta(x)\,\rho^{n}\,n^{-3/2}\,.

For such yy, recalling that xmx_{m} is the mthm^{\textrm{th}} element on π⁡(e,x)\pi(e,x),

x−1​y=a−ika−ik−1⋯a−im+1⏟x−1​xm​ajm+1ajm+2⋯ajn⏟xm−1​y.x^{-1}y=\underbrace{a_{-i_{k}}a_{-i_{k-1}}\cdots a_{-i_{m+1}}}_{\displaystyle x^{-1}x_{m}}\underbrace{a_{j_{m+1}}a_{j_{m+2}}\cdots a_{j_{n}}}_{\displaystyle x_{m}^{-1}y}\,.

γ⁡(x−1​y)γ⁡(y)→1,as ​y→ξ.\frac{\gamma(x^{-1}y)}{\gamma(y)}\to 1\,,\quad\text{as }\;y\to\xi.

C. Bounded range random walk on free groups
The result of this sub-section generalises the previous one.

(3.12) Theorem.

Suppose that the probability measure μ\mu on 𝔽\mathbb{F} has finite support SS which generates 𝔽\mathbb{F} as a semi-group and contains the group identity. Then the ratio limit compactification coincides with ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification analytically. Geometrically, it is the end compactification.

This needs some preparation. From Lalley [23], it is known that the random walk satisfies again a local limit theorem (1.6) with α=3/2\alpha=3/2, and ρ<1\rho<1 by non-amenability of 𝔽\mathbb{F}. We shall use a mix of the methods of [10] and its extensions by Picardello and Woess [24], and of [23], compare with [29, §19.B and §26.A].

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, let let Bn={x:|x|≤n}B_{n}=\{x:|x|\leq n\} be the ball of radius nn around the identity (root) with respect to the metric of the tree 𝕋\mathbb{T} which is the Cayley graph of the group. For any y∈𝔽y\in\mathbb{F}, the set y​BnyB_{n} is the ball of radius nn centred at yy. Let R=max⁡{|x|:x∈S}R=\max\{|x|:x\in S\}, and let B=BRB=B_{R}\,. For any set A⊂𝔽A\subset\mathbb{F}, we consider the stopping time plus associated probability generating function

where u,v∈𝔽u,v\in\mathbb{F}. For the simple proof of the following, see the above references.

If x0,x1∈𝔽x_{0}\,,x_{1}\in\mathbb{F} are distinct and y∈π⁡(x0,x1)y\in\pi(x_{0}\,,x_{1}) then the random walk starting at x0x_{0} must pass through y​ByB in order to reach x1x_{1}\,. Thus,

F⁡(x0,x1|z)=∑v∈y​BFy​B​(x0,v|z)​F​(v,x1|z).F(x_{0}\,,x_{1}|z)=\sum_{v\in yB}F^{yB}(x_{0}\,,v|z)F(v,x_{1}|z).

where u,u′∈Au,u^{\prime}\in A. There is N≥RN\geq R such that

where, as above, r=1/ρr=1/\rho. (This is a simple observation: there must be a sequence u=u0,u1​…,uk=vu=u_{0}\,,u_{1}\,\dots,u_{k}=v such that p⁡(ui−1,ui)>0p(u_{i-1}\,,u_{i})>0 for all ii. (3.14) 𝐅⁡(x,y|z)=(Fy​B​(x​u,y​v|z))u,v∈B,𝐟⁡(x,y|z)=(Fy​B​(x,y​u|z))u∈B​ and ​𝐠​(x,y|z)=(G⁡(x​u,y|z))v∈B.\begin{gathered}\mathbf{F}(x,y|z)=\bigl(F^{yB}(xu,yv|z)\bigr)_{u,v\in B}\,,\\ \mathbf{f}(x,y|z)=\bigl(F^{yB}(x,yu|z)\bigr)_{u\in B}\and\mathbf{g}(x,y|z)=\bigl(G(xu,y|z)\bigr)_{v\in B}.\end{gathered}

be its projection onto the standard simplex over BB (all non-negative vectors whose coordinates sum up to 11). Then the above yields the following, see [10], [24] or [29, §26.A].

4. Hyperbolic groups

We briefly recall the basic definition of hyperbolicity in the sense of Gromov [20]. Let (𝒳,d)(\mathcal{X},d) be a geodesic metric space, i.e., for any pair of points x,y∈𝒳x,y\in\mathcal{X}, there is a (not necessarily unique) geodesic π⁡(x,y)\pi(x,y), that is, an isometric embedding [0,d⁡(x,y)]↪𝒳[0\,,\,d(x,y)]\hookrightarrow\mathcal{X} which maps 00 to xx and d⁡(x,y)d(x,y) to yy. In our situation, 𝒳\mathcal{X} will carry the structure of a locally finite, connected graph and dd will be the graph metric. In this case, we replace the real interval [0,d⁡(x,y)][0\,,\,d(x,y)] by its integer counterpart [0,d⁡(x,y)]ℤ={0,1,…,d⁡(x,y)}[0\,,\,d(x,y)]_{\mathbb{Z}}=\{0,1,\dots,d(x,y)\}.

The metric space is called hyperbolic, if it is δ\delta-hyperbolic for some δ≥0\delta\geq 0 (possibly large): if a,b,c∈𝒳a,b,c\in\mathcal{X} and π⁡(a,b)\pi(a,b), π⁡(b,c)\pi(b,c), π⁡(c,a)\pi(c,a) are geodesics between the respective points (the sides of a triangle with vertices a,b,ca,b,c) then for every x∈π⁡(a,b)x\in\pi(a,b) there is y∈π⁡(b,c)∪π⁡(c,a)y\in\pi(b,c)\cup\pi(c,a) such that d⁡(x,y)≤δd(x,y)\leq\delta. The most basic examples are provided by trees, where δ=0\delta=0. For all our purposes, it will be convenient to assume without loss of generality that δ∈ℕ0\delta\in\mathbb{N}_{0} (non-negative integer).

We remark here that this implies, among many other facts, that any two geodesics connecting the same two points xx and yy are at Hausdorff distance at most δ\delta, and we let Π⁡(x,y)\Pi(x,y) denote the union of all those geodesics, a kind of “slim sausage”.

A finitely generated group Γ\Gamma is called hyperbolic, if its Cayley graph with respect to some finite, symmetric set of generators is hyperbolic. This does not depend on the specific generating set, up to a change of δ\delta. Basic examples are free groups and co-compact Fuchsian groups. The entire theory will not be repeated here. For the present purpose, the exposition in [29, §22] plus the references given there will suffice. Besides very basic cases (virtually cyclic groups), all infinite hyperbolic groups are non-amenable.

A locally finite hyperbolic graph 𝒳\mathcal{X}, resp. finitely generated hyperbolic group Γ\Gamma has its hyperbolic compactification 𝚫hyp​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{hyp}}(\mathcal{X}), resp. 𝚫hyp​(Γ)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{hyp}}(\Gamma). It was shown by Ancona [1] that under natural assumptions on PP on a hyperbolic graph 𝒳\mathcal{X} (bounded range, uniform irrecducibility; see [29, §27]), 𝚫hyp​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{hyp}}(\mathcal{X}) is a geometric realisation of the tt-Martin compactification for positive t>ρt>\rho. In the group case this has been progressively strengthened in papers by Gouëzel and Lalley:

(4.1) Theorem. [19], [17].

Let Γ\Gamma be a non-amenable, finitely generated hyperbolic group, and μ\mu a probability measure which induces an irreducible random walk. If μ\mu is symmetric and is finitely supported, then the tt-Martin compactification coincides with the 𝚫hyp​(Γ)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{hyp}}(\Gamma) for every t≥ρt\geq\rho.

If in addition, μ\mu is aperiodic, then the random walk satisfies a local limit theorem

p(n)(x,y)∼Cβ(x,y)ρnn−3/2as n→∞.p^{(n)}(x,y)\sim C\,\,\beta(x,y)\,\rho^{n}\,n^{-3/2}\quad\text{as }\;n\to\infty\,.

Regarding the Martin compactification, the noteworthy part is that it is also valid at the critical value t=ρt=\rho. The crucial tool for this is the following, whose part (a) was again first proved in [1] for z<r=1/ρz<r=1/\rho without requiring group-invariance, and then extended to z=rz=r in the group case in [19], [17], and finally [18], including the strong inequality (b).

(4.2) Proposition. (Ancona inequalities).

Suppose that Γ\Gamma and μ\mu are as in Theorem 4.1, and consider a Cayley graph of Γ\,\Gamma with respect to a finite, symmetric set of generators. Then there are constants CAnc≥1C_{\!\text{\rm Anc}}\geq 1 and 0≤α<10\leq\alpha<1 such that the following holds for all z∈[1,r]z\in[1\,,\,r].
(a) For any geodesic path π⁡(x,y)\pi(x,y) in the graph and any w∈π⁡(x,y)w\in\pi(x,y), one has

CAnc−1​G​(x,w|z)​G​(w,y|z)≤G⁡(x,y|z)≤CAnc​G​(x,w|z)​G​(w,y|z).C_{\!\text{\rm Anc}}^{-1}\,G(x,w|z)G(w,y|z)\leq G(x,y|z)\leq C_{\!\text{\rm Anc}}\,G(x,w|z)G(w,y|z)\,.

|G⁡(x,y|z)​G​(x′,y′|z)G⁡(x,y′|z)​G​(x′,y|z)−1|≤CAnc​G​(x,w|z)​G​(w,y|z)​αn.\left|\frac{G(x,y|z)G(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}|z)}{G(x,y^{\prime}|z)G(x^{\prime},y|z)}-1\right|\leq C_{\!\text{\rm Anc}}\,G(x,w|z)G(w,y|z)\,\alpha^{n}.

In order to get a feeling for the last inequality, observe that for a nearest neighbour random walk on a tree, one has α=0\alpha=0. As a matter of fact, it is proved in [18] that Proposition 4.2 and Theorem 4.1 are also valid when instead of finite support, one assumes that μ\mu has super-exponential moments, that is, ∑xa|x|​μ​(x)<∞\sum_{x}a^{|x|}\,\mu(x)<\infty for all a>1a>1.

(4.5) Theorem.

Let Γ\Gamma be a non-amenable, finitely generated hyperbolic group, and μ\mu a finitely supported symmetric probability measure which induces an irreducible & aperiodic random walk. Then the ratio limit compactification coincides with ρ\rho\,-Martin compactification analytically.

We note here that the last theorem does not fully cover the results on free groups and trees of §3. Theorem 3.3 does not need finite range, and Theorem 3.12 does not need symmetry, while symmetry of μ\mu is a crucial tool for the local limit theorem on hyperbolic groups stated in Theorem 4.1. In any case, it may be interesting to watch out how certain features of the respective proofs show up in different “disguise” in each of them.

5. Direct and Cartesian products

The ratio limit compactification adapts quite well to direct products. In general, let 𝚫⁡(𝒳1)\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{1}) and 𝚫⁡(𝒳2)\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{2}) be compactifications of the two discrete state spaces 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} and 𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{2}\,, with respective boundaries ∂𝒳1\partial\mathcal{X}_{1} and ∂𝒳2\partial\mathcal{X}_{2}\,. Then 𝚫⁡(𝒳1)×𝚫⁡(𝒳2)\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{1})\times\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{2}) is the natural associated compactification of 𝒳=𝒳1×𝒳2\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}\,. In this case, the boundary is

(5.1) ∂𝒳=(∂𝒳1×∂𝒳2)∪(𝒳1×∂𝒳2)∪(∂𝒳1×𝒳2).\partial\mathcal{X}=\bigl(\partial\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\partial\mathcal{X}_{2}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\partial\mathcal{X}_{2})\cup\bigl(\partial\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}).

We write elements of the product space as w1​w2w_{1}w_{2}\,, where wi∈𝚫⁡(𝒳i)w_{i}\in\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{i}). In the resulting topology, let (y1​(n)​y2​(n))n∈ℕ\bigl(y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence in 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Then, as n→∞n\to\infty\,,

y1​(n)​y2​(n)→ξ1​ξ2∈∂𝒳1×∂𝒳2⇔\displaystyle y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\to\xi_{1}\xi_{2}\in\partial\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\partial\mathcal{X}_{2}\iff yi​(n)→ξi​ in ​𝚫​(𝒳i)​ for ​i=1,2,\displaystyle y_{i}(n)\to\xi_{i}\;\text{ in }\;\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{i})\;\text{ for }\;i=1,2\,,
y1​(n)​y2​(n)→w1​ξ2∈𝒳1×∂𝒳2⇔\displaystyle y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\to w_{1}\xi_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\partial\mathcal{X}_{2}\iff y1​(n)=w1​for all but finitely many n, and\displaystyle y_{1}(n)=w_{1}\;\text{for all but finitely many $n$, and}
y2​(n)→ξ2​ in ​𝚫​(𝒳2),\displaystyle y_{2}(n)\to\xi_{2}\;\text{ in }\;\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{2})\,,
y1​(n)​y2​(n)→ξ1​w2∈∂𝒳1×𝒳2⇔\displaystyle y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\to\xi_{1}w_{2}\in\partial\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}\iff y1​(n)→ξ1​ in ​𝚫​(𝒳1), and\displaystyle y_{1}(n)\to\xi_{1}\;\text{ in }\;\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\mathcal{X}_{1}),\;\text{ and}
y2​(n)=w2​for all but finitely many n.\displaystyle y_{2}(n)=w_{2}\;\text{for all but finitely many $n$.}

Let us call this the product compactification of the given compactifications of 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} and 𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{2}\,, with the product boundary (5.1). Now let (𝒳1,P1)(\mathcal{X}_{1}\,,P_{1}) and (𝒳2,P2)(\mathcal{X}_{2}\,,P_{2}) the state spaces plus irreducible and aperiodic transition matrices of two respective Markov chains. Suppose that for i=1,2i=1,2

limn→∞pi(n)​(xi,yi)pi(n)​(ei,ei)=hi​(xi,yi)for all​xi,yi∈𝒳.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{p_{i}^{(n)}(x_{i}\,,y_{i})}{p_{i}^{(n)}(e_{i}\,,e_{i})}=h_{i}(x_{i}\,,y_{i})\quad\text{for all}\;x_{i},y_{i}\in\mathcal{X}\,.

The direct product is the Markov chain on 𝒳1×𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2} with transition matrix P=P1⊗P2P=P_{1}\otimes P_{2}, where

p⁡(x1​x2,y1​y2)=p1​(x1,y1)​p2​(x2,y2).p(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}y_{2})=p_{1}(x_{1}\,,y_{1})p_{2}(x_{2}\,,y_{2})\,.

It is clear that it has a ratio limit (1.1) with

h⁡(x1​x2,y1​y2)=h1​(x1,y1)​h2​(x2,y2),h(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}y_{2})=h_{1}(x_{1}\,,y_{1})h_{2}(x_{2}\,,y_{2}),

so that also the kernel H⁡(x1​x2,y1​y2)H(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}y_{2}) splits in the same way. The associated ratio limit compactification of 𝒳1×𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2} is not always the product compactification of the two ratio limit compactifications, but it is a factor thereof. The following is quite obvious; see e.g. the “preamble” on compactifications in [30, §7.B], and recall that the ratio limit compactification of 𝒳1×𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2} is the minimal one which provides continuous extensions of the functions H⁡(x1​x2,⋅)H(x_{1}x_{2}\,,\cdot), where x1​x2∈𝒳1×𝒳2x_{1}x_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}\,.

(5.2) Lemma.

Consider the extensions of Hi​(xi,⋅)H_{i}(x_{i}\,,\cdot) to the ratio limit boundary ℛi\mathcal{R}_{i} of 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i}\,, i=1,2i=1,2. For η=η1​η2\eta=\eta_{1}\eta_{2} and ζ=ζ1​ζ2∈(ℛ1×ℛ2)∪(𝒳1×ℛ2)∪(ℛ1×𝒳2)\zeta=\zeta_{1}\zeta_{2}\in\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{1}\times\mathcal{R}_{2}\bigr)\cup\bigl(\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{R}_{2})\cup\bigl(\mathcal{R}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}), let

η≈ζ⇔H1​(x1,η1)​H2​(x2,η2)=H1​(x1,ζ1)​H2​(x2,ζ2)for all ​x1​x2∈𝒳1×𝒳2.\eta\approx\zeta\iff H_{1}(x_{1}\,,\eta_{1})H_{2}(x_{2},\eta_{2})=H_{1}(x_{1}\,,\zeta_{1})H_{2}(x_{2},\zeta_{2})\quad\text{for all }\;x_{1}x_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}\,.

Then the ratio limit boundary ℛ\mathcal{R} of P=P1⊗P2P=P_{1}\otimes P_{2} is the image of the product boundary of the two ratio limit compactifications with respect to the factor map of the equivalence relation ≈\approx. In particular, the extension of H⁡(x1​x2,⋅)H(x_{1}x_{2}\,,\cdot) to ℛ\mathcal{R} is given by H⁡(x1​x2,ξ)=H1​(x1,η1)​H2​(x2,η2)H(x_{1}x_{2},\xi)=H_{1}(x_{1}\,,\eta_{1})H_{2}(x_{2},\eta_{2}), where η1​η2\eta_{1}\eta_{2} is a representative of the ≈\approx-equivalence class ξ\xi.

In a certain sense more natural than direct products are Cartesian products. Given PiP_{i} in 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i} for i=1,2i=1,2, write IiI_{i} for the identity operator (or matrix) over 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i} and choose a parameter s∈(0, 1)s\in(0\,,\,1). On 𝒳=𝒳1×𝒳2\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1}\times\mathcal{X}_{2}\,, let

P=Ps=s⋅P1⊗I2+(1−s)⋅I2⊗P2.P=P_{s}=s\cdot P_{1}\otimes I_{2}+(1-s)\cdot I_{2}\otimes P_{2}\,.

That is, the new Markov chain is such that first a coin is tossed where “heads” comes up with probability ss, and in that case, a step is performed according to P1P_{1} in tb first coordinate, while the second coordinate remains unchanged. And with probability 1−s1-s, a step is performed according to P2P_{2} in the second coordinate, while the first one remains unchanged.

For example, simple random walk on ℤd1+d2\mathbb{Z}^{d_{1}+d_{2}} arises as a Cartesian (and not direct) product of the simple random walks on ℤd1\mathbb{Z}^{d_{1}} and ℤd2\mathbb{Z}^{d_{2}} with s=d1/(d1+d2)s=d_{1}/(d_{1}+d_{2}).

In general, it does not appear to be completely straightforward that a ratio limit for each PiP_{i} also implies one for the Cartesian products PsP_{s}\,. However, the following was proved by Cartwright and Soardi [7].

(5.3) Proposition.

Suppose that each 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i} satisfies a local limit theorem of the form

pi(n)​(xi,yi)∼βi​(xi,yi)​ρin​n−αias ​n→∞,p_{i}^{(n)}(x_{i},y_{i})\sim\beta_{i}(x_{i},y_{i})\,\rho_{i}^{n}\,n^{-\alpha_{i}}\quad\text{as }\;n\to\infty\,,

where ρi=ρ⁡(Pi)\rho_{i}=\rho(P_{i}) for i=1,2i=1,2. Then one has for P=PsP=P_{s} that ρ=ρ⁡(P)=s​ρ1+(1−s)​ρ2\rho=\rho(P)=s\,\rho_{1}+(1-s)\,\rho_{2}\,,

p(n)​(x1​x2,y1​y2)∼C​β1​(x1,y1)​β2​(x2,y2)​ρn​n−α1−α2,p^{(n)}(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}y_{2})\sim C\,\beta_{1}(x_{1},y_{1})\beta_{2}(x_{2},y_{2})\,\rho^{n}\,n^{-\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}}\,,

where C=θα1​(1−θ)α2C=\theta^{\alpha_{1}}(1-\theta)^{\alpha_{2}}\,, with θ=s​ρ1/ρ\theta=s\rho_{1}/\rho.

In particular, in this case the ratio limit kernel for the Cartesian product is also H⁡(x1​x2,y1​y2)=H1​(x1,y1)​H2​(x2,y2)H(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}y_{2})=H_{1}(x_{1}\,,y_{1})H_{2}(x_{2}\,,y_{2}), and the ratio limit boundary is the same as for the direct product.

At this point, there is a natural question. Suppose that the ρi\rho_{i}\,-Martin boundary of PiP_{i} coincides with the respective ratio limit boundary for i=1,2i=1,2. Is this then also true for the ρ\rho-Martin boundary for the direct, resp. Cartesian products? So far, there is no general answer; the general problem lies in ρ\rho-Martin kernels of the product which are not minimal ρ\rho-harmonic functions. Some examples are known. We present three of them, which illustrate different situations regarding the equivalence relation ≈\approx that appears in Lemma 5.2. All three examples are valid for direct as well as Cartesian products, and the answer to the above question is “yes”.

(5.4) Example.

Suppose that 𝒳i=ℤdi\mathcal{X}_{i}=\mathbb{Z}^{d_{i}} and that the respective irreducible, aperiodic random walk is induced by a finitely supported probability measure μi\mu_{i}\,. Let hi​(x)=exp⁡⟨ci,x⟩h_{i}(x)=\exp\langle c_{i}\,,x\rangle be the unique ρi\rho_{i}\,-harmonic exponential on ℤdi\mathbb{Z}^{d_{i}}. That is, the vector cic_{i} minimises c↦∑xμi​(x)​exp⁡⟨c,x⟩c\mapsto\sum_{x}\mu_{i}(x)\exp\langle c\,,x\rangle, where c∈ℝdic\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}}, and the value of that minimum is the corresponding spectral radius ρi\rho_{i}\,. Every positive ρi\rho_{i}\,-harmonic function on ℤdi\mathbb{Z}^{d_{i}} is a constant multiple of hih_{i}, and in the ratio limit theorem, one has by a slight abuse of notation hi​(x,y)=hi​(x−y)h_{i}(x,y)=h_{i}(x-y). Thus, Hi​(x,y)=hi​(x)H_{i}(x,y)=h_{i}(x) for x∈ℤdix\in\mathbb{Z}^{d_{i}}, and the ratio limit kernel H⁡(x1​x2,y1​y2)=h1​(x1)​h2​(x2)H(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}y_{2})=h_{1}(x_{1})h_{2}(x_{2}) of the direct product also does not depend on y1​y2.y_{1}y_{2}\,. That is, the equivalence relation ≈\approx of Lemma 5.2 has a single equivalence class.

In this case, one also knows that all the involved compactifications coincide analytically with the Martin compactifications at the respective spectral radii. ∎

(5.5) Example.

Let 𝒳1=𝕋\mathcal{X}_{1}=\mathbb{T}, the regular tree with degree q+1≥3q+1\geq 3, and 𝒳2=ℤ\mathcal{X}_{2}=\mathbb{Z}. On each of the two, we consider “lazy” simple random walk, that is,

p1​(x1,x1)\displaystyle p_{1}(x_{1}\,,x_{1}) =12​ and ​p1​(x1,y1)=12​q+2​ when ​x1∼y1,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\;\text{ and }\;p_{1}(x_{1}\,,y_{1})=\tfrac{1}{2q+2}\;\text{ when }\;x_{1}\sim y_{1}\,,
p2​(x2,x2)\displaystyle p_{2}(x_{2}\,,x_{2}) =12​ and ​p2​(x2,y2)=14​ when ​x2∼y2,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\;\text{ and }\;p_{2}(x_{2}\,,y_{2})=\tfrac{1}{4}\;\text{ when }\;x_{2}\sim y_{2}\,,

while all other transition probabilities are 00. Then H1​(x1,y1)=Φ⁡(x1,y1)H_{1}(x_{1}\,,y_{1})=\Phi(x_{1}\,,y_{1}), see §3.A, and H2​(x2,y2)=1H_{2}(x_{2}\,,y_{2})=1. The ratio limit compactification of ℤ\mathbb{Z} is the one-point compactification ℤ∪{∞}\mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}, and the ratio limit boundary of the product space 𝕋×ℤ\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{Z} is 𝚫ends​𝕋\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}{\mathbb{T}}\,. Convergence to the boundary of a sequence (y1​(n)​y2​(n))n∈ℕ\bigl(y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is as follows, where K1(⋅,⋅|ρ1)K_{1}(\cdot,\cdot|\rho_{1}) is the Martin kernel on 𝕋\mathbb{T} given by (3.4)

y1​(n)→ξ1∈∂𝕋,y2​(n)​arbitrary\displaystyle y_{1}(n)\to\xi_{1}\in\partial\mathbb{T}\,,y_{2}(n)\;\text{arbitrary} ⇒H⁡(x1​x2,y1​(n)​y2​(n))→K1​(x1,ξ1|ρ1),\displaystyle\Rightarrow H\bigl(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)\to K_{1}(x_{1}\,,\xi_{1}|\rho_{1})\,,
y1​(n)=y1∈𝕋​for all ​n≥n0,|y2​(n)|→∞\displaystyle y_{1}(n)=y_{1}\in\mathbb{T}\;\text{for all }\;n\geq n_{0}\,,\;|y_{2}(n)|\to\infty ⇒H⁡(x1​x2,y1​(n)​y2​(n))→Φ⁡(x1,y1)Φ⁡(o1,y1).\displaystyle\Rightarrow H\bigl(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)\to\frac{\Phi(x_{1}\,,y_{1})}{\Phi(o_{1}\,,y_{1})}.

In particular, by Crotti [9], the ratio limit compactification coincides analytically with the ρ\rho-Martin compactification; see [29, Thm. 28.8]. In that reference, the result is stated for Cartesian products; the proof carries over to direct products with some obvious modifications. ∎

(5.6) Example.

Let 𝒳i=𝕋i\mathcal{X}_{i}=\mathbb{T}_{i} be two regular trees with respective degrees qi+1≥3q_{i}+1\geq 3. On each of the two, we consider “lazy” simple random walk as above, that is,

pi​(xi,xi)=12​ and ​pi​(xi,yi)=12​qi+2​ when ​xi∼yi,p_{i}(x_{i}\,,x_{i})=\tfrac{1}{2}\;\text{ and }\;p_{i}(x_{i}\,,y_{i})=\tfrac{1}{2q_{i}+2}\;\text{ when }\;x_{i}\sim y_{i}\,,

while all other transition probabilities are 00. Then Hi​(xi,yi)=Φi​(xi​yi)H_{i}(x_{i}\,,y_{i})=\Phi_{i}(x_{i}\,y_{i}), the spherical function on the respective tree as in §3.A. The ratio limit compactification of the direct or any Cartesian product of the two random walks is the product compactification of the ratio limit compactifications of the two trees. Convergence to the boundary of a sequence (y1​(n)​y2​(n))n∈ℕ\bigl(y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is as follows, where Ki(⋅,⋅|ρi)K_{i}(\cdot,\cdot|\rho_{i}) is the Martin kernel on 𝕋i\mathbb{T}_{i} given by (3.4)

y1​(n)→ξ1∈∂𝕋1,y2​(n)→ξ2∈∂𝕋2\displaystyle y_{1}(n)\to\xi_{1}\in\partial\mathbb{T}_{1}\,,\;y_{2}(n)\to\xi_{2}\in\partial\mathbb{T}_{2}
⇒H⁡(x1​x2,y1​(n)​y2​(n))→K1​(x1,ξ1|ρ1)​K2​(x2,ξ2|ρ2),\displaystyle\Rightarrow H\bigl(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)\to K_{1}(x_{1}\,,\xi_{1}|\rho_{1})K_{2}(x_{2}\,,\xi_{2}|\rho_{2})\,,
y1​(n)=y1∈𝕋1​for all ​n≥n0,y2​(n)→ξ2∈∂𝕋2\displaystyle y_{1}(n)=y_{1}\in\mathbb{T}_{1}\;\text{for all }\;n\geq n_{0}\,,\;y_{2}(n)\to\xi_{2}\in\partial\mathbb{T}_{2}
⇒H⁡(x1​x2,y1​(n)​y2​(n))→Φ1​(x1,y1)Φ1​(o1,y1)​K2​(x2,ξ2|ρ2),\displaystyle\Rightarrow H\bigl(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)\to\frac{\Phi_{1}(x_{1}\,,y_{1})}{\Phi_{1}(o_{1}\,,y_{1})}\,K_{2}(x_{2},\xi_{2}|\rho_{2})\,,
y1​(n)→ξ1∈∂𝕋1,y2​(n)=y2∈𝕋2​for all ​n≥n0\displaystyle y_{1}(n)\to\xi_{1}\in\partial\mathbb{T}_{1}\,,\;y_{2}(n)=y_{2}\in\mathbb{T}_{2}\;\text{for all }\;n\geq n_{0}
⇒H⁡(x1​x2,y1​(n)​y2​(n))→K1​(x1,ξ1|ρ1)​Φ2​(x2,y2)Φ2​(o2,y2).\displaystyle\Rightarrow H\bigl(x_{1}x_{2}\,,y_{1}(n)y_{2}(n)\bigr)\to K_{1}(x_{1},\xi_{1}|\rho_{1})\,\frac{\Phi_{2}(x_{2}\,,y_{2})}{\Phi_{2}(o_{2}\,,y_{2})}\,.

By [26], the ratio limit compactification coincides once more analytically with the ρ\rho-Martin compactification. Again, this holds for direct products in the same way as for Cartesian products. ∎

6. Reduced ratio limit compactification

The companion paper [11] makes crucial use of the following variant of the ratio limit compactification. Let ∼\sim be the equivalence relation on 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that

(6.1) y∼y′⇔H⁡(x,y)=H⁡(x,y′)for all ​x∈𝒳.y\sim y^{\prime}\iff H(x,y)=H(x,y^{\prime})\quad\text{for all }\;x\in\mathcal{X}\,.

We denote by 𝒳~\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} the set of equivalence classes, and by y~\tilde{y} the equivalence class of y∈𝒳y\in\mathcal{X}. Then the ratio limit kernel decends to a kernel on 𝒳×𝒳~\mathcal{X}\times\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} by

Hred​(x,y~)=H⁡(x,y).H_{\textrm{red}}(x,\tilde{y})=H(x,y).
(6.2) Definition.

The reduced ratio limit compactification33 3  [11] calls this the (ordinary) ratio limit compactification. 𝚫ratio​(𝒳~)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}) associated with 𝒳\mathcal{X} and PP satisfying (1.1) is the (up to homomorphism) unique compact Hausdorff space which contains 𝒳~\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} as a discrete, dense subset and has the following properties:

  • •

    for each x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, the function Hred​(x,⋅)H_{\textrm{red}}(x,\cdot) extends continuously to 𝚫ratio​(𝒳~)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}})\,, and denoting the extended kernel also by HredH_{\textrm{red}},

  • •

    if ξ,η∈ℛ⁡(𝒳~)=𝚫ratio​(𝒳~)∖𝒳~\xi,\eta\in\mathcal{R}(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}})=\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}})\setminus\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} are distinct, then there is x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} such that Hred​(x,ξ)≠Hred​(x,η)H_{\textrm{red}}(x,\xi)\neq H_{\textrm{red}}(x,\eta).

If 𝒳~\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} is finite then it is already compact, and there is no ratio limit boundary added to that space. The proofs of the following facts are easy exercises.

(6.3) Lemma.

(i) If the equivalence relation (6.1) is extended to all of 𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X}) via the extended ratio limit kernel on 𝒳×𝚫ratio​(𝒳)\mathcal{X}\times\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X}), then the resulting factor space is 𝚫ratio​(𝒳~)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}).
(ii) The factor map 𝒳→𝒳~\mathcal{X}\to\widetilde{\mathcal{X}} extends to a continuous surjection 𝚫ratio​(𝒳)→𝚫ratio​(𝒳~)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\mathcal{X})\to\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ratio}}(\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}) which is one-to-one from ℛ⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X}) into the reduced ration limit compactification.
(iii) If an equivalence class y~\tilde{y} is infinite, then it has a unique accumulation point ξ∈ℛ⁡(𝒳)\xi\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X}), and H⁡(x,y)=H⁡(x,ξ)H(x,y)=H(x,\xi) for all y∈y~y\in\tilde{y}.

If 𝒳=Γ\mathcal{X}=\Gamma is a countable group and PP is a random walk induced by a probability measure μ\mu, then

(6.4) Rμ={y∈Γ:H⁡(x,y)=H⁡(x,e)​ for every ​x∈Γ}R_{\mu}=\{y\in\Gamma:H(x,y)=H(x,e)\;\text{ for every }\;x\in\Gamma\}

is a subgroup of Γ\Gamma, see [11]. Since the ratio limit kernel h⁡(x,y)h(x,y) in (1.1) satisfies h⁡(x,y)=f⁡(x−1​y)h(x,y)=f(x^{-1}y), where f⁡(x)=h⁡(x,e)f(x)=h(x,e), one gets that

𝒳~(=Γred)=Γ/Rμ.\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}\;\bigl(=\Gamma_{\textrm{red}}\bigr)=\Gamma/R_{\mu}\,.

Elder and Rogers [14] have extended Avez’ Theorem 1.5: they show that for a symmetric, aperiodic random walk on an arbitrary finitely generated group, the set AμA_{\mu} of all y∈Γy\in\Gamma for which p(n)​(e,y)/p(n)​(e,e)→1p^{(n)}(e,y)/p^{(n)}(e,e)\to 1 is an amenable subgroup of Γ\Gamma. This implies at least in the symmetric case that Rμ⊂AμR_{\mu}\subset A_{\mu} is amenable.

(6.5) Proposition.

Consider a probability measure μ\mu on the finitely generated group Γ\Gamma which induces an irreducible & aperiodic random walk satisfying (1.1) and (1.2). Suppose that RμR_{\mu} is infinite, and that the associated element ξ∈ℛ⁡(𝒳)\xi\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{X}) according to Lemma 6.3(iii) is such that x↦H⁡(x,ξ)x\mapsto H(x,\xi) is a minimal ρ\rho-harmonic function.

Then Γ\Gamma fixes the boundary point ξ\xi.

Proof.

Like on the tt-Martin compactification, the group acts continuously on the ratio limit compactifictation, and the extended ratio limit kernel satisfies the cocycle identity

H⁡(g​x,ξ)=H⁡(x,g−1​ξ)​H​(g,ξ)for all ​x,g∈ΓH(gx,\xi)=H(x,g^{-1}\xi)H(g,\xi)\quad\text{for all }\,x,g\in\Gamma

(and of course for every boundary element, not only the ξ\xi of the statement).

By our assumptions, H⁡(x,y)=H⁡(x,e)=h⁡(x,e)=f⁡(x)H(x,y)=H(x,e)=h(x,e)=f(x) for all y∈Rμy\in R_{\mu}, and as |y|→∞|y|\to\infty, we have y→ξy\to\xi in the topology of the ratio limit compactification. Thus, f⁡(x)=H⁡(x,ξ)f(x)=H(x,\xi) for all x∈Γx\in\Gamma. By (1.2), the function

fˇ​(x)=f⁡(x−1)=h⁡(e,x)\check{f}(x)=f(x^{-1})=h(e,x)

satisfies f​P=ρ⋅ffP=\rho\cdot f, where PP is the transition matrix of the random walk. Using the cocycle identity, this can be rewritten as

H(x,ξ)=fˇ(x)=1ρ∑g∈Γμ(g)H(gx,ξ)=∑g∈Γμ⁡(g)​H​(g,ξ)ρ⏟=:cgH(x,g−1ξ)H(x,\xi)=\check{f}(x)=\frac{1}{\rho}\sum_{g\in\Gamma}\mu(g)H(gx,\xi)=\sum_{g\in\Gamma}\underbrace{\frac{\mu(g)H(g,\xi)}{\rho}}_{\displaystyle=:c_{g}}H(x,g^{-1}\xi)

for every x∈Γx\in\Gamma. Since ∑gcg=1\sum_{g}c_{g}=1, the minimality assumption on H⁡(⋅,ξ)H(\cdot,\xi) yields that H⁡(x,g−1​ξ)=H⁡(x,ξ)H(x,g^{-1}\xi)=H(x,\xi) for every x∈Γx\in\Gamma and every gg in the support of μ\mu. Therefore g​ξ=ξg\xi=\xi for every g∈𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉⁡(μ)g\in\operatorname{\sf supp}(\mu), and consequently for every g∈Γg\in\Gamma. ∎

(6.6) Corollary.

(a) For random walks on trees and free groups as considered in theorems 3.3 and 3.12, the subgroup RμR_{\mu} is trivial.
(b) For random walks on non-amenable hyperbolic groups as considered in Theorem 4.5, the subgroup RμR_{\mu} is finite. It is trivial when the group is torsion-free.

Statement (a) can of course also be seen from directly from the respective form of the extended ratio limit kernel, in particlar for the isotropic case. However, in the non-isotropic case, the present method is more convenient. Note that in all cases of the corollary, the ρ\rho-Martin boundary coincides with the minimal one. Furthermore, in all those cases, the entire group cannot fix a single boundary element: this has several different proofs, among which the author is best acquainted with [28, Prop. 4].

In examples 5.5 and 5.6, think 𝕋\mathbb{T} (even degree) as the free group. The repective random walks are of course induced be probabiliy measure on the respective product groups. In Example 5.5, we have Rμ={e1}×ℤR_{\mu}=\{e_{1}\}\times\mathbb{Z}, and the reduced ratio limit compactification is 𝚫ends​(𝕋)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{ends}}(\mathbb{T}). In Example 5.6, there is no reduction; RμR_{\mu} is trivial.

7. Final remarks

The above material should be seen as a collection of first answers to the question stated in the Introduction. The next step in the same direction would concern relatively hyperbolic groups, see the local limit theorem of [12]. Under the assumptions of that work, there is again a local limit theorem of the same form as for hyperbolic groups (see Theorem 4.1 above). It is not so easy to lay hands on the ratio limit kernel H⁡(x,y)H(x,y) in those cases, but one would expect that one also has that the ratio limit compactification coincides analytically with the ρ\rho-Martin compactification.

(7.1) Questions.

(a) Under which general conditions is it true that the ratio limit kernel is the left-sided limit H⁡(x,y)=G(2)​(x,y|r−)/G(2)​(e,y|r−)H(x,y)=G^{(2)}(x,y|r-)/G^{(2)}(e,y|r-) ?
(b) Under which general conditions does the corresponding compactification coincide analytically (or only geometrically) with the ρ\rho-Martin compactification ?

For relatively hyperbolic groups, in particular for free products of groups, there also are local limit theorems of the form (1.6), but with α>2\alpha>2, see Cartwright [5] and Candellero and Gilch [3]. This may be more challenging.

In the last decades there has not been much work on ratio limit theorems for random walks on groups; [14] is one of the interesting exceptions. On non-amenable groups, local limit theorems have prevailed. In a certain sense, the cases considered here might also be referred to as the “local limit boundary”. Indeed, apart from very few exceptions (e.g. radial random walks on trees), the author does not know of methods which provide a ratio limit theorem in the non-amenable environment without first proving a local limit theorem. This may indicate possibilities for future research.

More generally, let t≥ρ=ρ⁡(P)t\geq\rho=\rho(P), and suppose that we have a positive tt-harmonic kernel h⁡(x,y)h(x,y), that is, P​h​(⋅,y)=t⋅h⁡(⋅,y)Ph(\cdot,y)=t\cdot h(\cdot,y). In our situation, harmonicity is two-sided, i.e., we also have h⁡(x,⋅)​P=t⋅h⁡(x,⋅)h(x,\cdot)P=t\cdot h(x,\cdot). For example, if PP is the transition matrix of a random walk on a group Γ\Gamma induced by the probability measure μ\mu, then we may look for a solution of the convolution equation μ∗σ=t⋅σ\mu*\sigma=t\cdot\sigma (or the two-sided version) and set h⁡(x,y)=σ⁡(x−1​y)h(x,y)=\sigma(x^{-1}y). Then we can normalise by setting H⁡(x,y)=h⁡(x,y)/h⁡(e,y)H(x,y)=h(x,y)/h(e,y) and try to understand the corresponding compactification. If K(⋅,⋅|t)K(\cdot,\cdot|t) is the tt-Martin kernel of PP, then for each y∈𝒳y\in\mathcal{X} there is a probability measure νy\nu^{y} on ℳt​(𝒳)\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X}) such that

H⁡(x,y)=∫K⁡(x,ξ|t)​d​νy​(ξ).H(x,y)=\int K(x,\xi|t)\,d\nu^{y}(\xi)\,.

In the case when ℳt​(𝒳)\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X}) has only minimal boundary elements, the compactification induced by HH will coincide analytically with the tt-Martin compactification when for every ξ∈ℳt​(𝒳)\xi\in\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathcal{X})\,, one has that νy→δξ\nu^{y}\to\delta_{\xi} weakly as y→ξy\to\xi in 𝚫Mart,t​(𝒳)\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\textrm{Mart},\,t}(\mathcal{X}).
